q: Which list gives the steps of k-means in the correct order?
options: Place centres at random, assign points to the nearest centre, move centres to cluster means, repeat
Assign points to clusters, place centres at random, repeat until all clusters are the same size
Move centres to cluster means, place centres at random, assign points once and stop
Place centres at the data mean, label each point, then train a model on the labels
explain: K-means starts with random centres, assigns each point to the closest centre, moves each centre to the mean of its points, and repeats. It does not stop after one pass or need labels.

q: Why can you not simply pick the value of k that gives the lowest inertia?
options: Inertia is the same whatever value of k is used, so it cannot compare them
Inertia rises as k grows, so the smallest k would always be chosen
Inertia can only be worked out when k is two, so other values give no result
Inertia keeps falling as k grows, so the lowest value is always the largest k
explain: Inertia keeps falling as more clusters are added, so the lowest value would always point to the largest k. This is why the elbow, where improvement drops sharply, is used to choose k instead of the minimum.

q: Which clustering method groups points by density and can find clusters of arbitrary shape?
options: K-means
Hierarchical clustering
Gaussian mixture models
DBSCAN
explain: DBSCAN is density based and is good for irregular cluster shapes. K-means favours compact groups around centres.

q: What does principal component analysis do to a dataset?
options: It groups the points into a set number of clusters
It projects the data onto directions that capture the greatest variance
It predicts a label for each point from known examples that carry labels
It deletes the points that lie furthest from the mean
explain: Principal component analysis finds new axes, the principal components, along which the data varies most, and projects the data onto them. It is not a clustering or prediction method.

q: Compare supervised and unsupervised learning in terms of the data they use and what they aim to do.
model: Supervised learning uses labelled data, which are input and output pairs, and aims to predict outcomes for new data. Linear regression, decision trees and neural networks are examples. Unsupervised learning uses unlabelled data and aims to find inherent structure or patterns. K-means, principal component analysis and autoencoders are examples. For instance, supervised learning could predict house prices from past sales, while unsupervised learning could group customers by behaviour without any predefined groups.

q: Describe the main steps of principal component analysis and what the result is used for.
model: First the data is centred by subtracting the mean of each feature. Next the covariance matrix is calculated to show how features vary together. Eigen-decomposition of this matrix gives eigenvectors, which are the principal components, and eigenvalues, which show how much variance each carries. The data is then projected onto the chosen components. Keeping only the first few components gives a smaller summary that keeps most of the variance, which helps visualisation and can be useful before clustering.
points: Says eigenvectors give the components and eigenvalues give the variance
Says the data is projected onto the top components

q: Describe how the K-means clustering algorithm works. Explain how a suitable number of clusters can be chosen and how the quality of the clusters can be evaluated.
model: K-means is an unsupervised algorithm that groups unlabelled data into K clusters. It places K centroids, assigns each point to its nearest centroid, then moves each centroid to the mean of the points assigned to it. These two steps repeat until the assignments stop changing. Its aim is to minimise inertia, the sum of squared distances from each point to its cluster centre. To choose K, the elbow method plots inertia against K. Inertia always falls as K grows, and the elbow is where the improvement drops sharply, though it can be hard to see. The silhouette score compares how close each point is to its own cluster with how close it is to the nearest other cluster. A score near +1 means a good fit, so the K with the highest average score is a good choice.
points: Assigns each point to the nearest of K centroids
Moves each centroid to the mean of its points and repeats until stable
Elbow method plots inertia against K and picks the bend
Silhouette score, from -1 to +1, measures cluster quality, and the K that maximises it is chosen
Aim is to minimise inertia, the within-cluster sum of squared distances

q: What is the main objective of the K-means clustering algorithm?
options: Maximise the distance between every pair of observations
Minimise the within-cluster sum of squared distances
Maximise classification accuracy using labelled data
Minimise the number of features in the dataset
explain: K-means minimises inertia, the sum of squared distances from each point to its cluster centre. It uses no labels.

q: What does a silhouette score close to +1 mean for an observation?
options: The observation is likely assigned to an unsuitable cluster
The observation is equally close to two clusters
The observation is well matched to its cluster and separated from neighbouring clusters
The observation is an outlier in every possible clustering solution
explain: Near +1 means the point is much closer to its own cluster than to the nearest other one. Near 0 means it sits between two, and negative means it is probably in the wrong cluster.
